question: When does the umpire show a red card, and what happens next?

answer.reasoning: The question asks two things: when the umpire shows a red card, and what happens next. The Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) define the fault (red card) triggers in Law 16.7.1.2 and 16.7.1.3, and Law 16.7.2 states the consequence (report to the Referee, who may disqualify). The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) clause 5.17.4 gives the exact on-court procedure for showing the red card, and 5.17.5 plus 3.6.2.2 cover the disqualification (black card) outcome. answer.answer:
The umpire shows a red card when faulting a side for misconduct, which happens in two cases under Law 16.7.1 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26): (1) "faulting the offending side, if previously warned" (Law 16.7.1.2), or (2) "faulting the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach" (Law 16.7.1.3). These apply to breaches of Law 16.2, 16.4.1, 16.5.2 or 16.6 (Law 16.7.1).

The procedure (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.17.4): the umpire calls "Come here" to the offending player, then calls "… [name of player], fault for misconduct" followed by a specific explanation of the misconduct, "at the same time raising the right hand holding a red card above the Umpire's head. The Umpire must call the Referee on court and report immediately."

What happens next (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Law 16.7.2): "On faulting a side (Law 16.7.1.2 or 16.7.1.3), the umpire shall report the offending side immediately to the Referee, who shall have the power to disqualify the offending side from the match." If the Referee decides to disqualify, the umpire shows a black card instead and calls "… [name of player(s)], disqualified for misconduct" (ITTO 7.0 (5), clause 5.17.5); a disqualified player is disqualified from all events of the tournament (and in team tournaments from all future team matches), and a disciplinary process may be recommended in the Referee's Report (ITTO 7.0 (5), clause 3.6.2.2). As a fault, the offending side also loses the rally: Law 13.5 lists "if a player is guilty of flagrant, repeated or persistent offences under Law 16" as a fault, and Law 7.3 states "A side shall win a rally, if the opposing side commits a 'fault'".

answer.answer: Under Law 16.5.2 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, no player may leave the court during a match without the umpire's permission if doing so causes delay to play — the only exception is during the intervals described in Law 16.2. Those intervals are: not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points (Law 16.2.1), and not exceeding 120 seconds between the first and second game and between the second and third game (Law 16.2.2). The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) add that the umpire must ensure players do not leave the court without permission except during those intervals, or that when they do leave they do not delay play, and that a change of racket at courtside during a rally is permitted (Clause 5.10.1). If a player offends, the umpire reminds them that leaving the court needs permission and, if necessary, applies Law 16.7 (Clause 5.10.2): the umpire administers a breach of Law 16.5.2 by issuing a warning to the offending side, or by faulting the offending side if previously warned (Laws 16.7.1.1 and 16.7.1.2). So, to grab something mid-match, a player needs the umpire's permission and must not delay play; leaving freely is only allowed during the Law 16.2 intervals.
